subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on the role and functions of education, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain the role and functions of education for GCSE Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The functionalist view of the role and functions of education (Durkheim and Parsons)
The Marxist view of education (Bowles and Gintis)
Willis and the 'learning to labour' study of anti-school subcultures
Processes within school: labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy
Differential achievement by social class: material and cultural factors
Educational policies and the structure of education

questions.lo: The functionalist view of the role and functions of education (Durkheim and Parsons)
questions.q: Durkheim argued that a major function of education is to:
options: Prepare only the elite for university
Transmit society's shared norms and values and create social solidarity
questions.explain: Durkheim, a functionalist, argued education transmits shared norms and values and creates social solidarity, binding individuals into a 'society in miniature'.

questions.lo: The functionalist view of the role and functions of education (Durkheim and Parsons)
questions.q: Parsons described the school as a 'bridge' between the family and wider society because it teaches children to move from:
options: Particularistic standards judged on who you are, to universalistic standards judged by the same rules for all
questions.explain: Parsons argued the family judges children by particularistic standards, but school (and society) judge everyone by the same universalistic standards, so school acts as a bridge preparing pupils for the wider world.

questions.lo: The functionalist view of the role and functions of education (Durkheim and Parsons)
questions.q: A functionalist would argue that examinations perform the function of 'role allocation' because they:
options: Sift and sort pupils by ability so the most talented reach the most important roles
Prove that meritocracy is a myth
questions.explain: Functionalists (e.g. Davis and Moore, Parsons) argue education sifts and sorts pupils by ability. Exams allocate people to appropriate future roles, which they see as necessary and fair in a meritocracy.

questions.lo: The Marxist view of education (Bowles and Gintis)
questions.q: Bowles and Gintis argued that there is a 'correspondence principle' between school and work. This means that:
options: Schools have nothing in common with workplaces
The structures and relationships of school mirror those of the workplace, preparing an obedient workforce
questions.explain: Bowles and Gintis' correspondence principle argues school life mirrors working life (hierarchy, rewards, obedience). The hidden curriculum produces a docile, conformist workforce that suits capitalism.

questions.lo: The Marxist view of education (Bowles and Gintis)
questions.q: According to Bowles and Gintis, meritocracy is a 'myth' because:
options: Success actually depends heavily on class background, but education makes it look like it is based on ability
Every pupil genuinely has an equal chance
questions.explain: For Bowles and Gintis, the myth of meritocracy hides how class shapes success. It makes failure seem the pupil's own fault, legitimising and reproducing class inequality.

questions.lo: The Marxist view of education (Bowles and Gintis)
questions.q: A Marxist studying the hidden curriculum would be most interested in how schools teach pupils to:
options: Accept hierarchy, obey rules and become passive workers
questions.explain: Marxists argue the hidden curriculum instils obedience, acceptance of hierarchy and punctuality, producing conformist workers who accept their place in capitalist society.

questions.lo: Willis and the 'learning to labour' study of anti-school subcultures
questions.q: In his study 'Learning to Labour', Paul Willis found that the group of working-class boys he called 'the lads':
options: Formed an anti-school subculture and rejected school values, ending up in low-skilled jobs
Worked hard to gain qualifications and escape their class
Were passively brainwashed by the school with no resistance
questions.explain: Willis found 'the lads' actively formed a counter-school (anti-school) subculture that mocked school. Their resistance ironically prepared them for the very working-class jobs capitalism needed to fill.

questions.lo: Willis and the 'learning to labour' study of anti-school subcultures
questions.q: How does Willis's view differ from Bowles and Gintis?
options: Willis claims schools have no hidden curriculum
Willis stresses that pupils can actively resist school, not just passively accept its messages
Willis denies any link between education and capitalism
Willis argues education is fully meritocratic
questions.explain: Both are Marxist, but Willis emphasises pupil agency and resistance: 'the lads' actively rejected school. Bowles and Gintis portray pupils as more passively shaped by the correspondence principle.

questions.lo: Processes within school: labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.q: 'Labelling' in education refers to:
options: Writing pupils' names on their books
Teachers attaching a definition or judgement (e.g. 'bright' or 'troublemaker') to pupils
Grouping pupils by ability into sets
questions.explain: Labelling is when teachers categorise pupils, often based on assumptions about class, gender or ethnicity. These labels can influence how pupils are treated and how they come to see themselves.

questions.lo: Processes within school: labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.q: A teacher labels a pupil as 'lazy', gives them less attention, and the pupil then underachieves. This is an example of:
questions.explain: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when a label affects treatment and the pupil lives up (or down) to it. The negative label becomes true because of how it changes behaviour and expectations.

questions.lo: Pro-school and anti-school subcultures
questions.q: A 'pro-school subculture' is a group of pupils who:
options: Accept the school's values and aim to succeed through work and good behaviour
Reject the values of the school and misbehave
Leave school as early as possible
questions.explain: A pro-school subculture accepts and supports school values, working towards qualifications and conforming. An anti-school subculture does the opposite, rejecting school values.

questions.lo: Pro-school and anti-school subcultures
questions.q: Which process most often helps to explain why anti-school subcultures form?
options: Being placed in a low set and negatively labelled, leading pupils to seek status by rejecting school
questions.explain: Anti-school subcultures often form when pupils are placed in low sets and labelled as failures. Denied status through schoolwork, they gain status by opposing school rules and values.

questions.lo: Differential achievement by social class: material and cultural factors
questions.q: Which of the following is a MATERIAL factor explaining working-class underachievement?
options: Poor housing, low income and lack of study resources
questions.explain: Material factors concern money and physical resources: low income, overcrowded housing, and lack of books or a computer. Speech codes, labelling and cultural capital are cultural or in-school factors.

questions.lo: Differential achievement by social class: material and cultural factors
questions.q: Bernstein's idea that middle-class pupils are advantaged because school uses an 'elaborated code' of language is an example of a:
questions.explain: Language codes are a cultural factor. Bernstein argued schools use the elaborated code more familiar to middle-class pupils, disadvantaging working-class pupils who may mainly use a restricted code.

questions.lo: Differential achievement by gender
questions.q: One in-school explanation for girls generally outperforming boys at GCSE is:
options: Changes such as more positive teacher expectations of girls and girl-friendly assessment
Girls are labelled negatively more often
Girls have less access to education
questions.explain: Explanations for girls' higher achievement include changing teacher expectations, the impact of feminism on girls' ambitions, and assessment styles. External factors include expanded job opportunities for women.

questions.lo: Differential achievement by gender
questions.q: A sociologist argues boys' underachievement is partly due to a 'laddish' subculture where working hard is seen as uncool. This is best described as a:
questions.explain: A 'laddish' anti-learning subculture is a peer-group cultural factor within school. Pressure to appear masculine by not working hard can depress some boys' achievement.

questions.lo: Differential achievement by ethnicity
questions.q: The idea that the school curriculum reflects mainly the culture and history of the dominant ethnic group is called:
questions.explain: An ethnocentric curriculum prioritises the dominant group's culture and history, which can disadvantage or alienate minority ethnic pupils and is one in-school explanation for ethnic differences in achievement.

questions.lo: Differential achievement by ethnicity
questions.q: Which is an example of an OUT-OF-SCHOOL factor affecting achievement by ethnicity?
options: Material deprivation and higher poverty rates among some ethnic groups
questions.explain: Material deprivation at home (linked to higher poverty rates for some groups) is an out-of-school factor. Labelling, institutional racism and the ethnocentric curriculum are in-school factors.

questions.lo: Educational policies and the structure of education
questions.q: The introduction of a National Curriculum and league tables aimed to:
options: Guarantee equal outcomes for all pupils
Remove the state from education entirely
Standardise what is taught and increase competition and parental choice between schools
questions.explain: Policies such as the National Curriculum standardised content, while league tables and open enrolment aimed to raise standards through competition and parental choice (marketisation of education).

questions.lo: Educational policies and the structure of education
questions.q: Which criticism is often made of marketisation policies such as league tables and parental choice?
options: They only apply to private schools
They can advantage middle-class parents who are better placed to choose 'good' schools, widening inequality
questions.explain: Critics argue marketisation benefits middle-class families with the resources and knowledge to secure places at high-performing schools, so choice policies can widen rather than reduce class inequality.
